If the parse * succeeds, the return value is the new text position. Note that the parse * may succeed without fully reading the text and in this case those fields * that were read will be set. *

The failure is most likely caused by:

`org.joda.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.parseInto(org.joda.time.ReadWritableInstant, java.lang.String, int)`

Why:
- The exception occurs later when `DateTimeParserBucket` applies parsed fields, but the problematic setup happens in `parseInto`.
- `parseInto` computes:
  - `instantLocal = instantMillis + chrono.getZone().getOffset(instantMillis)`
  - `defaultYear = chrono.year().get(instantLocal)`
  - then creates `DateTimeParserBucket(instantLocal, chrono, ..., defaultYear)`
- `DateTimeParserBucket.computeMillis` explicitly injects that default year when parsing starts with month/day fields.
- For these tests, parsing `"2 29"` should preserve the supplied instant’s year context and accept Feb 29 in leap year 2004. Instead, field application reaches a state where `dayOfMonth=29` is validated against February with max 28, meaning the parsing base/default-year handling is wrong for this partial parse scenario.

Supporting static evidence:
- `BasicMonthOfYearDateTimeField.set` clamps day-of-month if needed.
- `SavedField.set` then applies day-of-month strictly.
- The thrown error `Value 29 for dayOfMonth must be in the range [1,28]` shows the bucket is applying the parsed fields against a non-leap-February context.
- Since `computeMillis` only injects the year and applies fields in sorted order, the root cause is upstream in how `parseInto` chooses the local base/default year for the bucket.

" * Parses a datetime from the given text, at the given position, saving the * result into the fields of the given ReadWritableInstant. If the parse * succeeds, the return value is the new text position. Note that the parse * may succeed without fully reading the text and in this case those fields * that were read will be set. *

* Only those fields present in the string will be changed in the specified * instant. All other fields will remain unaltered. Thus if the string only * contains a year and a month, then the day and time will be retained from * the input instant. If this is not the behaviour you want, then reset the * fields before calling this method, or use {@link #parseDateTime(String)} * or {@link #parseMutableDateTime(String)}. *

* If it fails, the return value is negative, but the instant may still be * modified. To determine the position where the parse failed, apply the * one's complement operator (~) on the return value. *

* This parse method ignores the {@link #getDefaultYear() default year} and * parses using the year from the supplied instant based on the chronology * and time-zone of the supplied instant. *

* The parse will use the chronology of the instant. * * @param instant an instant that will be modified, not null * @param text the text to parse * @param position position to start parsing from * @return new position, negative value means parse failed - * apply complement operator (~) to get position of failure * @throws UnsupportedOperationException if parsing is not supported * @throws IllegalArgumentException if the instant is null * @throws IllegalArgumentException if any field is out of range "

m41.content:
The failure is most likely caused by:

`org.joda.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.parseInto(org.joda.time.ReadWritableInstant, java.lang.String, int)`

Why:
- The exception occurs later when `DateTimeParserBucket` applies parsed fields, but the problematic setup happens in `parseInto`.
- `parseInto` computes:
  - `instantLocal = instantMillis + chrono.getZone().getOffset(instantMillis)`
  - `defaultYear = chrono.year().get(instantLocal)`
  - then creates `DateTimeParserBucket(instantLocal, chrono, ..., defaultYear)`
- `DateTimeParserBucket.computeMillis` explicitly injects that default year when parsing starts with month/day fields.
- For these tests, parsing `"2 29"` should preserve the supplied instant’s year context and accept Feb 29 in leap year 2004. Instead, field application reaches a state where `dayOfMonth=29` is validated against February with max 28, meaning the parsing base/default-year handling is wrong for this partial parse scenario.

Supporting static evidence:
- `BasicMonthOfYearDateTimeField.set` clamps day-of-month if needed.
- `SavedField.set` then applies day-of-month strictly.
- The thrown error `Value 29 for dayOfMonth must be in the range [1,28]` shows the bucket is applying the parsed fields against a non-leap-February context.
- Since `computeMillis` only injects the year and applies fields in sorted order, the root cause is upstream in how `parseInto` chooses the local base/default year for the bucket.

Dynamic verification was attempted but was inconclusive due debugger environment failure, not because the hypothesis was disproven. Static analysis still points to `DateTimeFormatter.parseInto(...)` as the buggy method.
